key_insight: At Re = 1000, a hemispherical leading-edge protuberance produces thicker vortical regions and shedding onset at 5°, while a simple flat plate achieves better glide ratios at 5°, 10°, and 15°.
engineering_relevance: Leading-edge geometry can guide aerodynamic design choices for small unmanned aerial or aquatic vehicles operating at low Reynolds numbers.
method: Two-dimensional numerical flow simulations at Re = 1000.
Compared a simple flat plate with a plate featuring a hemispherical leading-edge protuberance.
Examined vortex shedding, frequencies, and aerodynamic forces over angles of attack from 0° to 25°.
evidence_signal: Simulations show multiple force-coefficient frequencies at higher angles of attack and comparable glide ratios between the two geometries at higher angles.
watch_item: Results are limited to two-dimensional simulations at one Reynolds number; three-dimensional and experimental validation would be needed before vehicle-scale application.
paper_title: Effect of leading edge geometry on aerodynamic performance of a flat plate
